description_ru: О том, как пчёлы сообщают друг другу, где найти нектар, и как целая семья принимает общие решения.
text:
In 1973, an Austrian scientist named Karl von Frisch shared a Nobel Prize for a discovery that had taken him almost forty years. He had proved that honeybees possess a form of symbolic communication, one of the very few known in the animal kingdom outside our own species. The bees do not use sounds or words. They use a dance, and its meaning is so precise that a human observer can read it and find the flowers the bees have been visiting.

A honeybee colony is a remarkable society. In summer, a single hive may contain fifty thousand workers, all of them daughters of one queen. Different workers are given different jobs, and these change during their lives. Young bees clean the cells and feed the larvae, middle-aged bees build wax and guard the entrance, and the oldest ones, which are generally about three weeks old, become foragers who fly out to collect nectar and pollen.

Finding food is not easy. Flowers are scattered over an area of several square kilometres, and they bloom and fade according to the weather. Each morning, scout bees leave the hive without any information, and some of them return with nectar from a promising patch. What happens next is the extraordinary part. Inside the dark hive, the successful forager climbs onto the vertical surface of the honeycomb and begins to dance.

The most informative version is called the waggle dance. The bee walks forward in a straight line while shaking her body rapidly from side to side, then circles back to the starting point and repeats the movement, alternating between the left and the right loops. The straight section, known as the waggle run, carries the message. Its duration tells the others how far away the flowers are. The longer the run, the greater the distance, with roughly one second corresponding to about a kilometre.

The direction is communicated in an equally ingenious way. Because the hive is dark and the dance takes place on a vertical wall, the bee cannot point towards the flowers. Instead, she uses gravity as a reference. If she waggles straight upward, the food is in the direction of the sun. If she waggles at an angle of forty degrees to the right of vertical, the flowers lie forty degrees to the right of the sun. Remarkably, the bees even correct the angle as the sun moves across the sky.

The audience stays close to the dancer, touching her with their antennae, and they pick up the odour of the flowers that clings to her body. Then they fly out and search, using the dance as a map and the smell as a clue. It is worth remembering that these insects have brains smaller than a sesame seed. Their ability to carry out this task shows that complicated behaviour does not require a large brain, only a well-organised system.

Not every dance is a waggle dance. When the food is very close, within perhaps fifty metres, a forager performs a simpler round dance, which tells the audience only that flowers are nearby and invites them to search in every direction. The change to the waggle dance happens gradually as the distance grows, and some scientists suspect that the round dance is the older form from which the more precise language evolved.

The dance also helps a colony make decisions. In late spring, when a hive becomes overcrowded, about half of the bees leave with the old queen and form a swarm, which hangs from a branch while scouts look for a new home. Each scout returns and dances for the site she has found, and the better the site, the longer and more energetic her performance. Gradually, other scouts visit the sites that are most strongly advertised and then dance for them too.

Eventually, one site attracts so many supporters that a kind of quorum is reached, and the whole swarm takes off together. The biologist Thomas Seeley, who studied this process in detail, observed that the bees make the right choice, in the sense of choosing the best cavity, in the great majority of cases. There is no leader, and no individual understands the whole situation. The wisdom comes from the group, and it has been described as a democracy without politicians.

All this matters beyond curiosity. Honeybees, together with wild bees and other insects, pollinate many of the crops that people depend on, and it is estimated that roughly a third of the food we eat benefits from their work. In recent years, colonies have been weakened by disease, pesticides and the loss of wild flowers, and scientists are using the dance as a tool to study where bees find food and what damage has been done to their environment.

Von Frisch once said that the life of bees was like a magic well: the more you draw from it, the more it fills with water. Eighty years after his early experiments, researchers are still discovering new details, and each one confirms that a creature the size of a fingertip can teach us a great deal about information, cooperation and the way a society can think.

focus_sounds.tip_ru: Губы округлены, как для «у», затем быстро раскрываются; зубы не касаются губы.
Верхние зубы касаются нижней губы, голос включён; это не «ф» и не «у».
Долгий звук с нейтральным положением языка, губы не округлены; в американском варианте звучит «r».
Язык у мягкого нёба, звук идёт через нос; не добавляйте «г» в конце.

questions.question: What prize did Karl von Frisch share in 1973?
What does the length of the waggle run tell the other bees?
questions.answer: How far away the flowers are.

questions.question: How do bees show direction on a vertical wall?
questions.answer: They use the angle from vertical to represent the angle from the sun.

questions.question: How does a swarm choose a new home?
questions.answer: Scouts dance for sites, and the best-advertised one reaches a quorum.
